# Education in New Zealand
The education system in New Zealand has its origins in Māori traditional knowledge transfer and early European missionary schools. Māori education initially involved oral teaching by elders (tohunga) focused on tribal history and customs. European-style formal schooling began in 1815, with missionary schools teaching primarily in the Māori language initially. A national, secular, free, and compulsory education system was established starting in 1878, influenced by provincial models like Canterbury.
Early childhood education includes teacher-led centres (kindergartens, licensed services) and whānau-led services (Kohanga Reo, Playcentre), all licensed or certified by the Ministry of Education and guided by the curriculum framework Te Whāriki. Primary and secondary education is free for residents aged 5 to the end of the calendar year after their 19th birthday, with compulsory attendance from 6 to 16 years. Primary education spans Years 1–8 (ages 5–13), including an intermediate phase (Years 7–8); secondary education covers Years 9–13 (ages 13–18). School terms run from late January to mid-December with four terms and holiday breaks. The national curriculum applies to state and state-integrated schools, covering English/Māori language, mathematics, the arts, health, science, social sciences, technology, and languages, with assessments via the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) from Year 11. Parents may request exemption from sexuality education components.
Three school funding types exist: state (fully government-funded), state-integrated (government-funded but charge attendance dues for capital costs while retaining "special character"), and private schools (mainly tuition-funded). Most students attend state schools (~85%), with about 10% in state-integrated, and 4% in private schools. School enrolment schemes define home zones to manage overcrowding, which has socio-economic implications due to property value inflation. Homeschooling is allowed under strict exemptions.
Māori language education has been progressively supported, with Māori-medium schools (Kura Kaupapa Māori) providing immersion education. Though Māori language use declined due to historical policies restricting it, revitalization efforts and legislation have re-established it as an official language in education. Māori students in Māori-medium schools outperform their peers in mainstream schooling.
Tertiary education covers all post-school education and training, regulated by the New Zealand Qualifications Framework. Funding combines government subsidies and student fees, with students accessing loans and allowances. Concerns exist over rising fees and associated skill shortages. Educational standards showed declines in international assessments during the early 2000s but New Zealand remains relatively well-regarded globally. Addressing achievement gaps among Māori and Pacific Island students is an ongoing focus.
Bullying is a recognized concern, with reports of high incidence leading to government action including funding for positive behavior initiatives, though challenges remain with policy consistency across schools.
